nameStory: The Atlantic Sea Nettle gets its name from the stinging sensation it delivers, much like being brushed by a stinging nettle plant. The word 'nettle' comes from the Old English word meaning 'to sting,' and sailors have long used this comparison to describe the burning, irritating feeling of touching these jellies.
description: The Atlantic Sea Nettle is a graceful jellyfish that drifts through New England's coastal waters like an underwater parachute. Its bell-shaped body is typically pale, pinkish, or yellowish, often decorated with radiating stripes that become more vivid near the edges. Long, trailing tentacles stream beneath the translucent bell, which can pulse rhythmically as the jelly moves through the water. This species is smaller than its Pacific cousin but still makes an impressive sight when encountered in the ocean.

idTips.label: Bell coloration
idTips.description: Look for a translucent, dome-shaped bell that's pale pink, yellow, or whitish, often with darker radiating stripes that intensify toward the bell's edge like spokes on a wheel

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Long, ribbon-like tentacles trail from the bell's margin, feeling smooth and slippery to the touch (though you should never touch them due to stinging cells)

idTips.label: Bell shape
idTips.description: The bell has a classic mushroom or umbrella shape with a smooth, gelatinous texture that appears almost glass-like when backlit by sunlight

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with rhythmic, pulsing contractions of the bell, creating a hypnotic pumping motion as it drifts with the current

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than Pacific sea nettles, with the bell typically fitting within the span of your outstretched hand

habitat: Atlantic Sea Nettles drift in the open waters along New England's Atlantic coast, from nearshore areas to deeper offshore waters. They're most commonly spotted from boats, piers, or beaches during calm weather when the water is clear. These jellies prefer saltwater environments and are often seen floating near the surface where sunlight filters through the water.

seasonality.spring: Early arrivals may begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, though sightings are still relatively rare.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Atlantic Sea Nettle encounters, when warmer water temperatures bring them closer to shore and swimming areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but begin to become less common as water temperatures drop and storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters during the cold winter months, having moved to deeper or more southern waters.

funFact: Atlantic Sea Nettles were scientifically confused with other jellyfish species for decades, and it wasn't until 2017 that scientists finally sorted out that the Bay Nettle was actually a completely separate species that had been lumped together with Atlantic Sea Nettles all along!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative the Bay Nettle, which was only recognized as a separate species in 2017. Bay Nettles are typically found in more brackish, estuarine waters, while Atlantic Sea Nettles prefer full saltwater environments. Memory trick: Atlantic Sea Nettles stay in the Atlantic's full-salt waters.
contextualKnowledge: The Atlantic Sea Nettle has a complicated taxonomic history, having been confused with several other Chrysaora species for many years. This led to incorrect reports of Atlantic Sea Nettles from other oceans and regions where they don't actually occur, making older field guides and references potentially unreliable for this species.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the Bay Nettle, the Atlantic Sea Nettle prefers full marine saltwater rather than the brackish estuarine waters favored by Bay Nettles. Atlantic Sea Nettles also tend to have more variable coloration patterns and are generally found in more open ocean environments rather than protected bays and estuaries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bay Nettles are virtually identical in appearance to Atlantic Sea Nettles, but they prefer different salinity levels - Bay Nettles thrive in the brackish water of estuaries while Atlantic Sea Nettles prefer full ocean salinity.
